1. Proceedings in the present case have arising in filing of Dar in Fir No.221/2017 of Ps Gtb

4.

6.

Respondent no.3 filed the reply to the Dar taking an objection that present claim proceedings are
not maintainable against him as he was not registered owner of vehicle no. Dl-5Cf-2625.

It is
pleaded that vehicle no. Dl-5Cf-2625 was neither in his possession nor was b
eing driven by respondent no.3 on 03.09.2017, as such respondent no.3 is not liable for the claim.
Registered owner (respondent no.2) is liable for the same as vehicle was still registered in his name with transport authority.

It is pleaded that in 2015 respondent no.3 was only working as a valuer with M/s Himgiri Cars Private Limited and respondent no.2 had purchased a new vehicle in exchange to offending vehicle no.DL-5CF-2625 under a scheme.

At the time of the exchange, respondent no.2 had assured the company that he would transfer his vehicle on the record of transport authority in the name of M./s Himgiri Cars Private Limited, for which respondent no.3 had signed the relevant documents.

It is stated that on 30.09.2015 M/s Himgiri Cars Pvt. Ltd sold vehicle no. DL-5CF-2625 to Harmeet Singh (respondent no.4) and handed over all the original papers executed by respondent no.2, for the purpose of transfer of vehicle.
7. Reply has been filed by respondent no.4 who has also denied all the facts alleged in the DAR and stated that he has not been involved in MACT No.98/2018 Page 4 the accident.
It is pleaded that vehicle no.DL-5CF-2625 is not registered in his name.

8. On the basis of facts came on record ld. Predecessor of this Tribunal vide order dated 09.05.2018 framed following issues:
(1)Whether respondent no.2 was driving the offending vehicle No.DL- 5CF-2625 on 03.09.2017 at 7.30 pm at before Shahdara flyover, MS Park Metro Station, Delhi, in rash and negligent manner and caused the death of deceased Kameshwar Prasad?
OPP (2)Whether petitioners are entitled for compensation, if so, to what extend and from whom?
OPP (3)Relief.
9. In order to substantiate their case petitioners have examined two witnesses.
PW1 is petitioner Reeta Devi wife of deceased Kameshwar Prasad Yadav.
PW2 is Naresh Prasad who is eye witness to the accident.
On behalf of respondents, respondent no.2 Shailender Kumar has appeared as RW2.

No evidence has been led on behalf of respondent no.1, 3 and 4.
10.

I have heard Sh.B.N. Thakur, ld. counsel for petitioner, Sh.Pawan Kumar Sharma, ld. counsel for respondent no.1, Sh.Sanjeev Kumar, ld. counsel for respondent no.2 as well as Sh.Deepak Kumar Dhingra, ld. counsel for respondent no.3.
I have also gone through written submissions.

3 Issue No.1 11.
It is the settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of MACT No.98/2018 Page 5 evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
12.

sentences.text: PW1 Reeta Devi wife of deceased had stated that on 03.09.2017 her husband Kameshwar Prasad Yadav met with an accident while coming back to home after finishing his work.
PW1 was admittedly not eye witness to the accident.
PW2 Naresh Prasad has testified that he working as a labourer on daily wage basis and on 03.09.2017 he was coming from Apsara Border to Shahdara side from his work on his cycle.
Another cycle was ahead of him on flyover, by 50 feet distance.

PW2 says that he saw one Wagon R bearing registration no. DL-5CF-2625 came from the right side of PW2 and was being driven in a very rash and negligent manner and hit the cyclist who was going ahead of him on cycle.
PW2 stated that accident was caused by Wagon R car no. DL-5CF-2625 by its driver by driving in a very high speed and rash and negligent manner.
PW2 was not cross examined by respondent no.1/driver.

Although PW2 was cross examined at length by other respondents,
however nothing substantive could come in the cross examination.

13. Beside the oral testimony of PW2, the documents of DAR including recovery of offending vehicle no. DL-5CF-2625 in an accidental condition, response of respondent no.1 to notice u/s 133 M.V. Act,
post mortem report of deceased.
Mechanical inspection report of offending vehicle no.DL-5CF-2625.
All these documents also establish that deceased MACT No.98/2018 Page 6 died due to accidental injuries.
Post mortem doctor opined the cause of death to be shock as a result of ante mortem injuries, on head, chest, abdomen by blunt force impact.

Thus in view of the unrebutted testimony of PW2 coupled with other material available on judicial record, it is well established that deceased received accidental injuries in an accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no.1.
As such issue stands decided in favour of petitioners and against the respondents.
Issue No.2 14
. In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.

Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.

A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).

4 COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION 15.
The present case pertains to the death of deceased Kameshwar Prasad Yadav.

In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.

entities.text: Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Further, the guidelines have been reiterated by the Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case titled as National Insurance Company vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.

entities.text: National Insurance Company vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Decided on 31.10.2017,
laying down the general principles for computation of MACT No.98/2018 Page 7 compensation in death cases.

The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
"18.
There will be lesser need for detailed evidence.
It will also be easier for the insurance companies to settle accident claims without delay.

19. To have uniformity and consistency, the Tribunals should determine compensation in cases of death, by the following well-settled steps:
Step-1 (Ascertaining the multiplicand)
The income of the deceased per annum should be determined.
Out of the said income a deduction should be made in regard to the amount which the deceased would have spent on himself by way of personal and living expenses.
The balanc expired e which is considered to be the contribution to the dependent family, constitutes the multiplicand.
Step-2 (Ascertaining the multiplier)
Having regard to the age of the deceased and period MACT No.98/2018 Page 8 of active career, the appropriate multiplier should be selected.

This does not mean ascertaining the number of years he would have lived Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
5 or worked but for the accident.
Having regard to several imponderables in life and economic factors, a table of multipliers with reference to the age has been identified by this Court.
The multiplier should be chosen from the said table with reference to the age of the deceased.
Step-3 (Actual Calculation)

The annual contribution to the family(multiplicand)
when multiplied by such multiplier gives the 'loss of dependency' to the family.
Thereafter, a conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000/- to Rs.10,000/- may be added as loss of estates.
Where the deceased is survived by his widow, another conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000 to Rs.10,000 should be added under the head of loss of consortium.
But no amount is to be awarded under the head of pain, suffering or hardship caused to the legal heirs of the deceased.

The funeral expenses, cost of transportation of the body (if incurred) and the cost of any medical treatment of the deceased before death (if incurred) should also be added."
16.

Therefore, in view of the aforesaid judgment, it is essential to take into consideration the following parameters:-
PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
Age of deceased :
17.
PW1 Reeta Devi, wife of the deceased in her evidence has deposed that her husband was of age of about 42 years at the time of accident and proved original Aadhar card of deceased as Ex.PW1/A.
Perusal of Aadhar card Ex.PW1/A of deceased shows that year of birth of deceased was 1975.
As such on the date of accident i.e. on 03.09.2017, MACT No.98/2018 Page 9 deceased was proved to be of 42 years of age.
This fact is also reflected from post mortem report of deceased.

Assessment of Income of deceased :
18.
In order to prove the income of the deceased PW1 testified that his husband deceased Kameshwar Prasad Yadav was working as a cooker maker at a monthly salary of Rs.15,000/- per annum.
PW1 also deposed that deceased was earning all his income for supporting his legal heirs/dependents.
During cross-examination PW1 stated that her deceased husband was working with someone who was dealing in copper and he was earning Rs.15,000/- per month.
PW1 stated that she has no document to prove that her husband was working or was drawing salary of Rs.15,000/- per month.

Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
6 19.
No documentary evidence has been placed on record by the petitioners to prove the work and income of the deceased.

In the absence of any cogent evidence or material, this Tribunal is of the view that petitioners have failed to prove that deceased was working as a cooker maker or that he used to earn Rs.15,000/- per month at the time of his death.

In the absence of any such material this Tribunal assesses income of deceased to be at parity with minimum wages of unskilled worker in Delhi which at the time of accident was of Rs.13,584/- per month.

Application of Multiplier:
20.
As held above, deceased was about 42 of age at the time of accident.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.
The judgment titled as Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121 is relevant to consider the multiplier.

In Para 21 of the judgment, the guidelines for the multiplier were laid down in accordance with age are as under:
MACT No.98/2018 Page 10  MULTIPLIER AGE GROUP OF DECEASED  M-18 Age group between 15 to 20 & 21  to 25 years)
 M-17 Age group between 26 to 30 yrs  M-16 Age group between 31 to 35 yrs  M-15 Age group between 36 to 40 yrs  M-14 Age group between 41 to 45 yrs  M-13 Age group between 46 to 50 yrs  M-11 Age group between 51 to 55 yrs  M-9 Age group between 56 to 60 yrs  M-7 Age group between 61 to 65 yrs  M-5 Age group between 66 and above 21.
In view of the above, multiplier of 14 has to be applied against the age bracket of 41 to 45 years to determine the compensation.

Future Prospects:
22.
This issue was considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Pranay Sethi & Others (Supra).

Relevant parts of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
"(iii) While determining the income, an addition of 50% of actual salary to the income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below the age of 40 years, should be made.
The addition should be 30%, if the age of the deceased was between 40 to 50 years.
In case the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years, the addition should be 15%.
Actual salary should be read as actual salary less tax.

(iv) In case, the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40%
of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
7 age of 40 years.

An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years MACT No.98/2018 Page 11 and 10% where the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.

The established income means the income minus the tax component."
23.

Since on the day of accident deceased was aged around 42 years, in view of said fact this Tribunal finds that 25% of the income of deceased (aged between 40 to 50 years) has to be considered towards future prospects.

Deduction towards Personal Living Expenses:
24.
After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards his personal expenses.

Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Anr., (2013) 9 SCC 65, in para 30, laid down the necessary deductions towards personal living and expenses of deceased as under :
 Deductions out of earning of the Number of  deceased dependents  Where dependent is 1 Half  Where the number of dependent family 1/3rd  members is 2 to 3  Where the number of dependent family 1/4th  members is 4 to 6  Where the number of dependent family 1/5th  members exceeds 6 (six)
25.

sentences.text: Instant claim petition has been filed by four petitioners i.e. widow and minor children of deceased.
Since, the deceased was survived by four dependents, one-fourth of the income of the deceased is to be MACT No.98/2018 Page 12 deducted towards his personal living expenses.

NON-PECUNIARY DAMAGES:
26.

In case of Pranay Sethi (Supra), a compensation of Rs.40,000/-, 15,000/- and Rs.15,000/-
respectively has been fixed on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses.

Therefore, a compensation of Rs.40,000/-, 15,000/- and Rs.15,000/- respectively on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses is required to be granted and further, it is required to be enhanced @ 10% in every three years.

Therefore, a compensation of Rs.48,000/-,
18,000/- and Rs.18,000/- respectively on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses is required to be granted.

Further, in view of recent decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as United India Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Satinder Kaur @ Satwinder Kaur & Ors., Civil Appeal no. 2705 of 2020, decided on 30.06.2020, loss of consortium has to be fixed for each of the Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
8 LRs.

Thus, petitioners in this case shall be entitled to a total compensation of Rs.23,71,480/- only.
INTEREST ON AWARD 29.
Petitioners shall also be entitled to interest @ 8% per annum on the award amount from the date of filing of the petition till realization.
LIABILITY 30.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondent is liable to pay the compensation amount.
As noted above the registered owner of the offending vehicle no.DL-5CF-2625 was Shailender Kumar who admittedly sold the said vehicle at Himgiri Auto India Pvt. Ltd. to respondent no.3 Kirpal Singh.

Respondent no.2 Shailender Kumar has appeared as RW2 and testified that he exchanged the offending vehicle no. DL-5CF-2625, while purchasing a car from M/s Hyundai Cars Ltd i.e. Grand I10 Magna registration no.DL 8CAM 4063.

At that time Hyundai Cars Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
9 Limited issued a receipt and delivery receipt dated 28.09.2015 Ex.RW1/A.

entities.text: Hyundai Cars Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
RW2 further states that respondent no.3 Kirpal Singh assured him that every care will be taken while dealing with offending vehicle no. DL-5CF-2625 and official got some papers signed from him for transfer of ownership of said vehicle.
31.
RW2 further deposed that later he came to know about the MACT No.98/2018 Page 14 accident in question.

Witness says that he had earlier visited 2/3 times to Hyundai showroom to enquire regarding transfer of ownership of offending vehicle but they gave one line reply that now it was their responsibility to deal with offending vehicle no. DL-5CF-2625.

RW2 further proved stamp ledger account sheet Ex.PW1/B.
32.

Having considered the evidence, first of all it be noted that two documents i.e. delivery receipt and ledger account details Ex.RW1/A and Ex.RW1/B respectively, though have been exhibited but these documents only are copies.
It be noted that mere exhibition of a document is not proof of the same.
Original document i.e. delivery receipt was required to be proved.
Moreover the delivery receipt does not bear the signature of RW2 at any point of time.
Nor the witness has stated in this regard.

Although this fact is not disputed even by respondent no.3 in pleadings that he being official of Himgiri Auto India Pvt. Ltd had purchased the offending vehicle under an exchange scheme for selling a new vehicle to respondent no.2.
But fact remains that the document Ex.RW1/A does not mention why the name of respondent no.2 has never been changed in the registration certificate of offending vehicle.

33. Hon'ble Apex Court in Surender Kumar Bhilawe vs. New India Assurance Company Limited 2020 SCC OnLine SC 523 has held that the person in whose name the vehicle is registered at the time of accident is considered to be the 'owner'.

entities.text: Surender Kumar Bhilawe vs. New India Assurance Company Limited 2020 SCC OnLine SC 523
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Hon'ble Apex Court while referring to definition of 'owner' as given in section 2(30) of M.V. Act, as well as referring to provisions of Section 39 to 41,
50, 51, 66, 69, 82(g), 86(c), 146, 157, 177 and 192(A) of M.V. Act, laid down that under the earlier definition of owner as defined under Section 2(19) of repealed M.V. Act 1939, owner meant the person in possession of the motor vehicle.

MACT No.98/2018 Page 15 However on account of change in the definition only registered owner would be considered to be the one who is liable for the compensation in case of said vehicle caused any accident.

It was further observed as "it is difficult to accept that a person who has transferred ownership of vehicle, on receipt of consideration, would not report the transfer or apply for transfer of registration, and thereby continued to incur the risk and liabilities of ownership of vehicle under the provisions of law, in particular under M.V. Act 1988 as well as other criminal/penal laws.....".
34. Hon'ble Supreme Court further referred to Section 157 of M.V. Act and the Explanation attached thereto, which provide regarding transfer of certificate of insurance.

Said section clearly provides that in case of transfer of certificate of insurance to another person, ownership of the motor vehicle in respect of which such insurance is taken together with policy of insurance, certificate of insurance and policy shall be deemed to have been transferred in favour of the person to whom the motor vehicle is transferred, with effect from date of transfer of certificate of insurance.

Explanation attached to section 157(1) clarifies that deemed transfer under the said provision shall include Dar-Reeta Devi vs Sanjeev Dixit on 13 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168711966/
10 transfer of right and liability from the date of certificate of insurance and policy.
35.

Thus the legal position has been made clear that the person who is registered as an owner of the vehicle, would be considered to be an owner for liability, unless the name has been transferred if the vehicle was sold.

Reference can also be given of another judgment of Apex Court in P.P. Mohammad vs. Rajappan (2008) 17 SCC 624.
36.

In this case even if it is admitted position that vehicle was sold by respondent no.2 to Himgiri Auto India Pvt. Ltd through its official/ respondent no.3 and thereafter that company sold the vehicle further to MACT No.98/2018 Page 16 respondent no.4 and respondent no.4 sold it to respondent no.1 and accident occurred from respondent no.1.
Fact remains that vehicle stood in the name of respondent no.2.

Therefore in the present case in view of the law as discussed above respondent no.2 being registered owner and respondent no.1 being driver of the offending vehicle (who was otherwise also in possession of vehicle), are liable jointly and severally to pay the amount of compensation.

No liability can be fixed for payment of compensation upon respondent no.3 and 4.
Relief 37.

This Tribunal awards a compensation of Rs.23,71,480/- to the petitioners along with interest @
8% per annum from the date of filing of petition till realization to be paid by respondent no.1 and 2 jointly and severally.
Amount of interim award, if any, be deducted from the compensation amount along with the waiver of interest, if any, as directed by the Tribunal during the pendency of this case.

The respondent no.1 and 2 are directed to deposit the award amount in A/c no.20780110171912 (IFSC Code UCBA0002078), UCO Bank, Karkardooma, Delhi, of PO MACT, Shahdara, through RTGS/ NEFT, within 30 days from today.
Respondent no.1 and 2 are also directed to give notice regarding deposit of the said amount to the petitioners.

8. On the basis of facts came on record ld. Predecessor of this Tribunal vide order dated 09.05.2018 framed following issues:
(1)Whether respondent no.2 was driving the offending vehicle No.DL- 5CF-2625 on 03.09.2017 at 7.30 pm at before Shahdara flyover, MS Park Metro Station, Delhi, in rash and negligent manner and caused the death of deceased Kameshwar Prasad?

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
No evidence has been led on behalf of respondent no.1, 3 and 4.
10.
It is the settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of MACT No.98/2018 Page 5 evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand & Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018 Law Suit (SC) 303.
12.
Thus in view of the unrebutted testimony of PW2 coupled with other material available on judicial record, it is well established that deceased received accidental injuries in an accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no.1.
As such issue stands decided in favour of petitioners and against the respondents.
. In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.
Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.
Further, the guidelines have been reiterated by the Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case titled as National Insurance Company vs. Pranay Sethi & Ors.
Having regard to several imponderables in life and economic factors, a table of multipliers with reference to the age has been identified by this Court.
The multiplier should be chosen from the said table with reference to the age of the deceased.

6 19.
No documentary evidence has been placed on record by the petitioners to prove the work and income of the deceased.
In the absence of any cogent evidence or material, this Tribunal is of the view that petitioners have failed to prove that deceased was working as a cooker maker or that he used to earn Rs.15,000/- per month at the time of his death.
In the absence of any such material this Tribunal assesses income of deceased to be at parity with minimum wages of unskilled worker in Delhi which at the time of accident was of Rs.13,584/- per month.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.
Since on the day of accident deceased was aged around 42 years, in view of said fact this Tribunal finds that 25% of the income of deceased (aged between 40 to 50 years) has to be considered towards future prospects.
After choosing the age, multiplier and income of the deceased, necessary deductions have to be made out of the income of the deceased towards his personal expenses.
Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Reshma Kumari & Ors. v. Madan Mohan & Anr., (2013) 9 SCC 65, in para 30, laid down the necessary deductions towards personal living and expenses of deceased as under :
 Deductions out of earning of the Number of  deceased dependents  Where dependent is 1 Half  Where the number of dependent family 1/3rd  members is 2 to 3  Where the number of dependent family 1/4th  members is 4 to 6  Where the number of dependent family 1/5th  members exceeds 6 (six)
25.
33. Hon'ble Apex Court in Surender Kumar Bhilawe vs. New India Assurance Company Limited 2020 SCC OnLine SC 523 has held that the person in whose name the vehicle is registered at the time of accident is considered to be the 'owner'.
Thus the legal position has been made clear that the person who is registered as an owner of the vehicle, would be considered to be an owner for liability, unless the name has been transferred if the vehicle was sold.
Reference can also be given of another judgment of Apex Court in P.P. Mohammad vs. Rajappan (2008) 17 SCC 624.
36.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Since, the deceased was survived by four dependents, one-fourth of the income of the deceased is to be MACT No.98/2018 Page 12 deducted towards his personal living expenses.
In case of Pranay Sethi (Supra), a compensation of Rs.40,000/-, 15,000/- and Rs.15,000/-
respectively has been fixed on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses.
Therefore, a compensation of Rs.48,000/-,
18,000/- and Rs.18,000/- respectively on account of loss of consortium, loss of estate and funeral expenses is required to be granted.
Since, the deceased was survived by four legal heirs, therefore, the claimants are entitled to a sum of Rs.2,28,000/- (48,000 X 4 + 18,000 + 18,000) under this head.
Therefore in the present case in view of the law as discussed above respondent no.2 being registered owner and respondent no.1 being driver of the offending vehicle (who was otherwise also in possession of vehicle), are liable jointly and severally to pay the amount of compensation.
No liability can be fixed for payment of compensation upon respondent no.3 and 4.
